Internship Details 
 
Roles: Field Application Engineer (FAE) and Technical Sales 
Associate (TSA) 
Both roles involve some aspects of sales. However, TSA leans 
more towards sales while FAE involves more technical aspects. 
 
Eligibility Criteria: 
CPI: 6.00+ 
Branches: EXTC, Electronics, Electrical 
 
Stipend: INR 50,000 /- per month plus a one-time relocation 
benefit of INR 25,000/- 
 
Location: Bangalore/Pune/Delhi. One important

3 
Online Assessment Test 
We were sent a registration link where we had to fill out basic personal 
details and select the preference for role (TSA/FAE/Both). I selected both. 
A couple of days before the test, we were sent documents containing job 
description of the roles and a prep guide for the interview. This guide 
contained all the information about the scope of the interview, their 
expectations from candidates, how to answer questions and even YouTube 
playlists and textbooks that the candidates should cover. This was the key 
to cracking this interview as the interview process very closely followed the 
prep guide.  
The online assessment had two sections: 
a. Technical (20 questions): This section had questions on all topics 
encompassing electrical syllabus including and not limited to 
Electrical Networks, Electrical Devices, Analog Devices, Amplifiers, 
Filters, Microprocessors, Control Systems, etc. The questions were of 
varying difficulty and types. One important thing to note is that there 
was a negative marking scheme of +1/-0.25. 
b. Aptitude (20 questions): This section had common aptitude style 
questions on comprehension, statistics, logical reasoning, etc.  
Interview Round 1 - TSA 
We received the list of shortlisted students three days before the interviews 
and I had been shortlisted for the TSA role. My interview was scheduled for 
5th September at 10:00am. The interviews were held offline at TPO.   
I entered the interview room and greeted the interviewer. He warmly 
greeted me back and asked me to introduce myself. I briefly spoke about

4 
my background, interests, and skills and named the projects I did that 
reflected the same. The interviewer quickly went through my resume and 
remarked that my resume suggests that I would be a better fit for FAE role 
and enquired about my interests on the same. I answered truthfully that I 
was inclined towards the FAE role as I am better at technical aspects. 
The interviewer then moved on to a couple of basic technical questions. 
After that, he went through my resume again, asking a few questions about 
my projects and interests. He also asked about the subjects that I had 
studied in my course. This was followed by a few sales and marketing 
related questions that were straightforward to answer.  
He then began with a roleplaying scenario in which he played the role of 
an unhappy customer who received the wrong resistors which has caused 
huge losses to him and I was to play the role of a TI sales executive. I was 
supposed to find a solution to this problem that would satisfy the customer 
and prevent losses to TI. I tried my best to placate the customer while 
finding an optimal solution. The roleplay lasted for a few minutes after 
which the interview was concluded. 
As I walked out of the interview room, my interviewer said that he feels I 
would be a good fit for the FAE role and would recommend me for the 
same. 
Interview Round 1 - FAE 
After my TSA interview, I was quickly called in for an FAE interview. Round 
1 of the FAE interview resembled more a viva exam than an interview. The 
interviewer very briefly looked at my resume and asked me to introduce 
myself. After that he asked me to draw circuits for certain converters. He 
asked me draw a couple of circuits that could be used to convert a high 
voltage AC source to a low voltage DC source. He questioned me on the 
components I used, specifically their V-I characteristics. He then drew a 
very complicated looking circuit that used MOSFETs and had an input of a 
square wave and asked me to draw the output. The circuit was very big and

5 
I needed some time to go through it. The interviewer left the room to give 
me some time. My answer was partially correct and he told me what the 
error was. 
The next few questions used BJT and once again I was told to find the 
output (waveform, voltage values, etc.). Some of these questions were very 
complicated looking but had a very simple solution to them. It is important 
to note that the interview did not focus much on the different 
configurations of semiconductor devices (common-emitter, common-base, 
common-collector, etc.). The basics of these semiconductor devices were 
far more important. 
The next couple of question involved the use of DC-DC converters (Buck, 
Boost). I was asked in detail about each component, their purpose, and 
their behavior in the circuits. And with that, the over hour-long interview 
concluded.  
Interview Round 2 – FAE 
Round 2 started the same as the previous rounds with a greeting an 
introduction. The interviewer went through my resume and asked 
questions on a couple of my projects. He asked to me explain an ML 
project I had done but did not ask ay further questions on it. 
The second project he asked about involved BLDC motors and I was 
extensively questioned on this project. Project details like the concept 
behind it, the chips used along with the reason for selecting them and 
details of the working of the chip. I was also asked electrical based 
questions about the project. This part of the interview was very in-depth 
and required a fair bit of thinking. Ensure that you are very thorough with 
all the projects you have mentioned on your resume. 
The interviewer then moved on to questions on the electrical syllabus. 
This part of the interview was more difficult than round 1 of FAE 
interview. The topics included DC-DC converters, Op-Amp, BJT, RLC

6 
circuits, passive filters, Three-phase converters, etc. This part of the 
interview was difficult because it required a very deep understanding and 
intuitive knowledge about each component involved. The questions were 
unique and required one to ponder for a minute to be able to answer. The 
important aspect of this part is that you need to keep walking the 
interviewer through the process. The interviewer needs to know that you 
are thinking in the correct manner even if you end up answering the 
question incorrectly. The interviewer even helped me through a couple of 
snags, making discussions about solutions easier. 
There was a point where the interviewer wanted to ask me questions 
about a topic that I didn’t know about. I told him the same and he quickly 
moved on to the next topic. This was an important point that the TI prep 
guide mentioned and it is certainly something to keep in mind during the 
interview. 
Another type of question that I was asked was to draw a block diagram of 
a mobile phone. Try to draw the diagram as detailed as possible with 
components like transducers, sensors, output devices, battery and its 
management systems, processor, etc. You might be asked some 
questions about different components and their working. 
The interviewer concluded with a final question about my willingness to 
move to Bangalore. Finally, he gave me some suggestions and areas to 
improve on.

7 
 
Tips: 
1. Go through the prep guide extremely well. It will be your best friend 
throughout the selection process as it outlines exactly what TI 
expects from you and what you should expect from the interviews. 
The prep guide also gives very good resources for you to study each 
topic. 
2. Ensure that your basics are clear and that you have an intuitive 
understanding. 
3. Keep walking the interviewer through your thought-process. 
4. Do not give up quickly. Working in the correct direction is more 
important than the answer. 
5. Be honest. Whether it is your preference for a role or lack of 
knowledge about a certain topic, be upfront about it. 
6. Don’t be intimidated by complex looking questions. Many of the 
questions asked had very straight-forward answer but had 
unnecessary complexity just to confuse the candidate.
